did_you_know.text: Did you know? Elihu uses the senses of the human body as an illustration of critically examining his words: the ear tests words, and the palate tastes food.
Did you know? Elihu suggests that the dispute be settled by jointly examining the arguments, in order to determine what is good and right between them.
Did you know? Elihu rejects the idea that evil or injustice can be attributed to God, emphasizing instead His holiness and righteousness.
Did you know? According to Elihu, God repays people according to their deeds and brings upon them the outcome of their ways.
Did you know? Elihu describes human life as dependent on the spirit and breath, which God can gather back to Himself.
Did you know? The chapter presents a general picture of human frailty: all flesh will perish, and people will return to the dust.
Did you know? Elihu emphasizes that God shows no partiality to princes and does not favor the rich over the poor, because all people are the work of His hands.
Did you know? Elihu says that God’s eyes are on people’s ways and that all their steps are visible to Him; therefore, there is no hidden place for those who do evil.
Did you know? Elihu presents God as the One who can bring quiet, hide His face, or bring change upon a nation or an individual alike.
Did you know? Elihu suggests that a person should turn to God by acknowledging their condition and asking for guidance, even saying, “If I have done wrong, I will not do so again.”
